candidate_datasets.name: Global Biodiversity Information Facility

candidate_datasets.name: WorldClim

candidate_datasets.name: Dryad

candidate_datasets.name: COMPADRE and COMADRE
candidate_datasets.role: population projection matrices for estimating demographic fitness consequences

candidate_datasets.name: NCBI Sequence Read Archive

candidate_datasets.role: phenotype and fitness data from natural-population studies

candidate_datasets.name: Global Register of Introduced and Invasive Species

candidate_datasets.name: Dryad

candidate_datasets.name: Dryad
candidate_datasets.role: stage-specific life-history, pedigree and selection datasets

candidate_datasets.name: Encyclopedia of Life TraitBank

candidate_datasets.name: Dryad

candidate_datasets.name: Encyclopedia of Life TraitBank

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life

candidate_datasets.name: TRY Plant Trait Database

candidate_datasets.name: NCBI Sequence Read Archive

candidate_datasets.name: TRY Plant Trait Database

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database

operationalization: Quantify how exceptional a species' trait is relative to congeners and relate that value to within-species trait variance, distinguishing species-specific from clade-wide novelty. A positive phylogenetically controlled association supports the rule.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoBank
candidate_datasets.role: comparative morphological characters among allied species

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: specimen-level anatomy for trait and variance estimates

candidate_datasets.name: Dryad
candidate_datasets.role: within-species morphometric datasets

obstacles: Most comparative trait datasets have too few individuals per species.
Defining an extraordinary degree across heterogeneous traits requires normalization.
rationale: The association is operationally clear after standardizing traits and has a straightforward refuting result. Public data can test selected animal groups, but not Darwin's broad scope or the stated plant uncertainty.

operationalization: For traits used in taxonomy, compare within-species variation of species-diagnostic characters with genus-shared characters after scaling and measurement-error correction. Greater variation in specific characters supports the claim; equal or lower variation refutes it.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoBank
candidate_datasets.role: taxonomic morphological character matrices

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: multiple specimens for quantitative character variation

candidate_datasets.name: NCBI GenBank
candidate_datasets.role: within- and among-species sequence variation

obstacles: Taxonomists may choose stable diagnostic characters, creating ascertainment bias.
Generic and specific characters differ in measurement scale and type.
rationale: The variance comparison is feasible in clades with rich specimen sampling. Global tests are constrained by inconsistent character coding and sparse within-species replication.

operationalization: Within genera or families, compare standardized among-species divergence and within-species variance for secondary sexual traits versus other morphology. Larger values for sexual traits support the claim; comparable or smaller divergence refutes it.

candidate_datasets.name: Macaulay Library
candidate_datasets.role: sex-labelled images and sounds for avian ornaments and displays

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: specimen-level sexually dimorphic morphology

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: phylogenetic control in among-species comparisons

obstacles: Trait classes need comparable scaling and sampling.
Public media and specimens are heavily biased toward birds and conspicuous traits.
rationale: This yields a standard comparative effect-size test and rich data exist for birds and some mammals. Secondary sexual traits and within-species variation are not comprehensively coded across animals.

operationalization: For pedigreed reappearance events, test whether causal ancestral alleles or regulatory states were transmitted cryptically through intervening generations and became expressed under particular genetic or environmental conditions. Demonstrated continuous transmission supports the claim; a genuinely new mutation producing the resemblance refutes it.

candidate_datasets.name: NCBI Sequence Read Archive
candidate_datasets.role: genomes and pedigrees from domestic breeds and mutant lines

candidate_datasets.name: Dryad
candidate_datasets.role: pedigree and genotype-phenotype datasets documenting trait reappearance

obstacles: Historical breed pedigrees and DNA over hundreds of generations are unavailable.
Reappearance can arise from retained alleles, epigenetics, recombination or new mutation.
rationale: Modern genetics can test Darwin's transmission model in documented recent cases. Existing data rarely span enough generations to distinguish all proposed routes for long-lost characters.

operationalization: Infer Equus relationships and reconstruct ancestral coat-pattern states using ancient and modern genomes, preserved pigmentation loci, fossil evidence and extant phenotype coding. A common ancestor with high posterior support for striping supports the claim; independent stripe origins or a confidently unstriped ancestor refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: NCBI GenBank
candidate_datasets.role: modern and ancient Equus sequence data

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: fossil Equus occurrences and taxonomy

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoBank
candidate_datasets.role: phylogenetic character matrices for fossil and extant equids

obstacles: Coat stripes are rarely preserved in fossils.
Ancient DNA does not reach the deepest Equus common ancestor and pigmentation genotype-phenotype mapping is incomplete.
rationale: Common ancestry is strongly testable, and ancestral striping can be probabilistically reconstructed. Direct evidence for the ancestral phenotype remains incomplete, so the full historical claim is not decisively resolvable.

operationalization: Under matched environmental perturbations, compare the direction and type of heritable phenotypic variation among close versus distant relatives. Greater parallel variation among close relatives, and resemblance of variants to congeneric species, supports the claim.

candidate_datasets.name: Dryad
candidate_datasets.role: common-garden, mutation and experimental-evolution phenotype datasets

candidate_datasets.name: NCBI Sequence Read Archive
candidate_datasets.role: genomic data for parallel variants and shared genetic architecture

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: relatedness for comparative analyses

obstacles: Similar phenotypes may reflect shared environment rather than inherited constitution.
Matched perturbation datasets across several related species are uncommon.
rationale: Parallel variation has clear comparative predictions and can be tested in selected radiations. Public data are scattered and seldom contain identical environmental exposures across an adequate phylogenetic design.

operationalization: In densely sampled lineage series, test whether appearance and improvement of derived forms precede decline and disappearance of inferred parents and intermediates. A repeated temporal replacement pattern supports the prediction; long coexistence or ancestor persistence refutes its generality.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: stratigraphic occurrences of putative lineage sequences

candidate_datasets.name: Neotoma Paleoecology Database
candidate_datasets.role: high-resolution occurrence time series for recent transitions

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoBank
candidate_datasets.role: morphological matrices for identifying derived and intermediate forms

obstacles: Direct ancestors and transitional varieties are hard to identify.
Replacement can be driven by environment rather than new-form competition.
rationale: Selected fossil series can test temporal replacement, but preservation and ancestry uncertainty are substantial. Existing data rarely distinguish extinction by competitive species formation from coincident turnover.

operationalization: Estimate range widths and overlap-zone widths for geographically replacing close relatives, and fit abundance changes toward each boundary. Overlap zones consistently narrow relative to each range and abrupt edge declines support the claim; broad overlap or gradual transitions refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: Global Biodiversity Information Facility
candidate_datasets.role: georeferenced occurrences for ranges and overlap zones

candidate_datasets.name: eBird
candidate_datasets.role: standardized abundance and occurrence data for representative bird species

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: identification of closely allied species pairs

obstacles: Occurrence density reflects observer effort as well as abundance.
Hybrid zones and patchy habitat complicate a single overlap-width measure.
rationale: The geometric and abundance predictions are direct and large public datasets provide broad coverage. Standard occupancy models can account for effort, allowing a decisive present-day test across many species pairs.

operationalization: Identify phenotypically or genetically intermediate natural populations and compare their abundance or occupancy with the two endpoint forms under standardized sampling. Lower abundance of intermediates across systems supports the claim; equal or greater abundance refutes it.

candidate_datasets.name: Global Biodiversity Information Facility
candidate_datasets.role: occurrence and specimen records for endpoint and named intermediate forms

candidate_datasets.name: NCBI Sequence Read Archive
candidate_datasets.role: population genomic data for identifying admixed or intermediate populations

candidate_datasets.name: Dryad
candidate_datasets.role: hybrid-zone abundance and phenotype datasets

obstacles: Intermediate varieties are inconsistently named and sampled.
Narrow range alone can create low total abundance without lower local fitness.
rationale: The abundance comparison is clear for documented clines and hybrid zones. A general assessment requires compiling scattered genotype and census data beyond what current integrated databases provide.

operationalization: Track common endpoint and rare intermediate populations for beneficial mutation supply, adaptive response and subsequent replacement. Faster adaptation proportional to population size followed by decline of intermediates supports the mechanism.

candidate_datasets.name: NCBI Sequence Read Archive
candidate_datasets.role: temporal population genomic datasets for adaptive allele appearance

candidate_datasets.name: Dryad
candidate_datasets.role: experimental evolution and hybrid-zone datasets with population sizes

obstacles: Rare populations differ from common ones in habitat, gene flow and drift.
Few datasets jointly observe mutation supply, adaptation and competitive replacement.
rationale: Each component has standard measurements and experimental systems can test the causal chain. Existing public data seldom contain the entire process in natural incipient species.

operationalization: Reconstruct bat ancestry using fossil-calibrated mammal phylogenies and compare ancestral forelimb and membrane characters with extant and fossil gliders. Transitional gliding-adapted anatomy predating powered-flight characters supports the claim; evidence for a non-gliding ancestor or alternative functional sequence refutes it.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: fossil bat and mammal occurrences and ages

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoBank
candidate_datasets.role: morphological phylogenetic matrices for fossil and living mammals

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: three-dimensional anatomy of bats and gliding mammals

obstacles: The earliest known bats were already capable of powered flight.
Soft flight membranes are rarely preserved and extant gliders are not necessarily ancestral analogues.
rationale: Public fossil and morphology resources permit explicit ancestral-state analyses. The critical transition is poorly sampled, so existing data can constrain but not decisively recover the origin of bat flight.

operationalization: Identify species whose observed habitat use or behaviour differs from that predicted by homologous structures and close relatives, then reconstruct whether behavioural shifts precede structural evolution. Repeated behavioural mismatch with retained ancestral anatomy supports the claim.

candidate_datasets.name: Macaulay Library
candidate_datasets.role: media documenting bird behaviour and habitat use

candidate_datasets.name: eBird
candidate_datasets.role: bird occurrence and habitat-use data

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: comparative anatomy for structures associated with habitat and locomotion

obstacles: Structure-function mismatch requires an explicit expectation model.
Present-day mismatch does not by itself establish the temporal order of habit and structural change.
rationale: Current behaviour and retained anatomy can be documented directly in many species. Existing data support the existence claim, but historical precedence usually requires uncertain ancestral reconstruction.
